q.s: While balancing her checkbook, Sofia sees that her bank statement includes a $5 monthly service fee that she has not recorded. What should Sofia do with the fee?
o: Subtract it from her check register balance
Add it to her check register balance
Subtract it from the bank statement balance
Ignore it until next month's statement
q.r: Subtract it from her check register balance. When the bank has already charged a fee, the bank statement balance is correct, but the account holder's own record is not. Service fees and other bank charges must be subtracted from the check register so it matches the bank's figure. Adding the fee would make her balance too high, subtracting it from the statement would count it twice, and ignoring it would leave her records wrong.
w: A service fee takes money out of the account, so adding it to the register would make Sofia's balance look higher than it really is.
The bank has already taken the fee out of its statement balance, so subtracting it there again would count the fee twice.
The fee has already been charged, so waiting until next month leaves Sofia's register showing more money than she actually has.

q.pt: Explain the nature of charitable giving
q.s: Before donating $200 to an organization that contacted her online, what should Carmen do first?
o: Give her bank account number so the gift can be withdrawn quickly
Verify that the charity is legitimate and see how it uses donations
Donate in cash so the organization receives the money sooner
Pay immediately because the request says the offer ends today
q.r: Verify that the charity is legitimate and see how it uses donations. Responsible charitable giving means confirming that a nonprofit is real and well run before giving. Donors can check whether it is a registered tax-exempt organization with the IRS and review how much of its spending supports its mission. Sharing bank account numbers, giving untraceable cash, and responding to high-pressure deadlines are common signs of charity scams.
w: Giving a bank account number to an organization that contacted her online is risky and is a common way charity scams steal money.
Cash gifts are hard to trace and leave a weak record for taxes, and speed is not the issue; Carmen first needs to know the charity is real.
A deadline saying the offer ends today is a high-pressure tactic often used in scams, so paying immediately skips the needed checking.

q.pt: Describe the need for financial information
q.s: A restaurant manager reviews monthly sales reports and notices that dessert orders have declined every month since spring. This shows that businesses use financial information to
q.r: Identify performance trends. Financial information, such as sales, expense, and profit reports, lets managers see patterns over time and make better decisions, such as changing the dessert menu or promotion. Spotting trends early helps a business increase sales and control costs. Businesses do not set government tax rates, no information can eliminate risk entirely, and financial reports do not replace the training employees need.
w: Businesses do not set government tax rates, so reviewing dessert sales reports cannot serve that purpose.
Financial information helps manage risk, but no report can eliminate business risk entirely, and the manager is spotting a pattern in sales.
Sales reports help managers make decisions, but they do not replace the training employees need to do their jobs.

q.pt: Describe the need for financial information
q.s: Ava's manager asks her to double-check that the expense figures in a report are complete, accurate, and free from bias before the report goes to investors. The manager wants the information to be
q.r: Reliable. Reliable financial information is accurate, complete, verifiable, and free from bias, so decision makers can trust it. Relevant information relates directly to the decision being made, timely information is available when it is needed, and comparable information can be measured against other periods or businesses. All are useful qualities, but checking that figures are accurate, complete, and unbiased focuses on reliability.
w: Relevant information relates directly to the decision being made, but Ava is checking whether the figures are accurate and unbiased, which is about trustworthiness.
Timely information is available when it is needed, while Ava's task is checking that the numbers are complete, correct, and free from bias.
Comparable information can be measured against other periods or companies, but the manager wants Ava to confirm the figures can be trusted.

q.pt: Describe the need for financial information
q.s: The owner of a lawn-care company is deciding whether to buy a second riding mower this month. Which financial information is most relevant to her decision?
o: The cost of supplies the company bought five years ago
The amount of last year's charitable donations
A competitor's sales goal for next year
The amount left in this year's equipment budget
q.r: The amount left in this year's equipment budget. Relevant financial information relates directly to the decision being made. Knowing how much money remains in the current equipment budget tells the owner whether the purchase is affordable now. Supply costs from five years ago are out of date, last year's donations have no bearing on equipment spending, and a competitor's sales goal is not information about the owner's own ability to pay.
w: Supply costs from five years ago are outdated and say nothing about whether the owner can afford a mower this month.
Last year's charitable donations have no connection to whether the company has money available now to buy equipment.
A competitor's sales goal describes another business's plans, not how much money the owner has to spend on a second mower.

q.pt: Explain the purposes and importance of credit
q.s: Isabella's store account lets her charge purchases up to $1,500, pay part of the balance each month, and keep making new purchases as she pays the balance down. This is an example of __________ credit.
q.r: Revolving. Revolving credit provides a credit limit that the borrower can use, repay, and use again, with interest charged on any unpaid balance and a minimum payment due each month; most credit cards and store accounts work this way. Installment credit is repaid in a set number of equal payments. Single-payment credit must be repaid in one lump sum, and trade credit is credit that suppliers give to businesses.
w: Installment credit is repaid in a set number of equal payments, while Isabella's account lets her keep reusing her credit limit as she pays it down.
Single-payment credit must be repaid in one lump sum, but Isabella pays part of her balance each month and keeps charging.
Trade credit is credit suppliers give to businesses, not a store account a consumer like Isabella uses for personal purchases.

q.pt: Explain the purposes and importance of credit
q.s: Marcus borrows money to buy a used car and agrees to repay it in 48 equal monthly payments that include interest. Marcus is using __________ credit.
q.r: Installment. Installment credit is a loan for a specific amount that is repaid, with interest, in a fixed number of equal payments over a set period. It is commonly used for costly items such as cars, furniture, and appliances. Revolving credit has a credit limit that can be reused as it is paid down, single-payment credit is repaid in one lump sum, and trade credit is extended by suppliers to business customers.
w: Revolving credit, like a credit card, has a limit you can reuse as you pay it down, while Marcus's car loan is a fixed amount with set payments.
Single-payment credit is repaid all at once in one lump sum, but Marcus is repaying the car loan in 48 monthly payments.
Trade credit is offered by suppliers to business customers, but Marcus is an individual borrowing money to buy a car.

q.pt: Explain the purposes and importance of credit
q.s: How does consumer credit benefit businesses?
o: It reduces the costs of billing and collection
It increases sales by letting customers pay later
It lowers the risk that customers will not pay
It allows businesses to charge lower prices
q.r: It increases sales by letting customers pay later. Credit lets consumers purchase goods and services before they have saved the full price, which increases demand, sales, and production for businesses and supports economic growth. Offering credit adds billing and collection costs and increases the risk that some customers will not repay. Credit does not lead to lower prices; borrowers usually pay interest.
w: Offering credit actually adds billing and collection work for a business, since it has to send bills and chase late payments.
Selling on credit raises the chance that some customers will never pay, so it increases rather than lowers that risk.
Credit does not make prices lower; customers who buy on credit usually end up paying interest on top of the price.

q.pt: Explain the role of finance in business
q.s: A growing software company sells shares of ownership to investors to raise money for a new product line. The company is using __________ financing.
q.r: Equity. Equity financing raises money by selling ownership shares in the business, such as stock, to investors; the money does not have to be repaid, but the investors gain a share of ownership and profits. Debt financing means borrowing money that must be repaid with interest. Trade financing involves credit from suppliers, and lease financing lets a business use an asset in exchange for regular payments without buying it.
w: Debt financing means borrowing money that must be repaid with interest, but this company is selling ownership shares instead.
Trade financing is credit from suppliers, not money raised by selling shares of ownership to investors.
Lease financing lets a business use an asset for regular payments, while this company is raising cash by selling ownership.

q.pt: Explain the role of finance in business
q.s: Which business function is responsible for obtaining money, managing it, and deciding how it will be used to help the business reach its goals?
q.r: Finance. Finance is the business function that obtains the funds a business needs, manages those funds, and decides how to invest them so the company can operate and grow. It includes activities such as budgeting, securing loans or investors, and managing cash. Marketing focuses on satisfying customers' wants and needs, operations produces goods and services, and human resources manages employees.
w: Marketing focuses on understanding and satisfying customers' wants and needs, not on getting money and deciding how the business will use it.
Operations handles producing goods and services day to day, while the question describes obtaining and managing the business's money.
Human resources manages hiring, training, and supporting employees, not raising funds or deciding how money is invested.

q.pt: Explain the role of finance in business
q.s: Managers at a manufacturing company compare the expected returns of three possible equipment projects to decide which long-term investment the company should fund. This activity is called
q.r: Capital budgeting. Capital budgeting is the finance activity of evaluating and selecting long-term investments, such as equipment, buildings, or new product lines, based on their expected costs and returns. Working capital management focuses on short-term assets and liabilities, such as cash, inventory, and accounts payable. Credit analysis judges whether a borrower is likely to repay, and payroll accounting records employee pay.
w: Working capital management deals with short-term items like cash and inventory, but these managers are choosing a long-term equipment investment.
Credit analysis judges whether a borrower will repay a loan, not which long-term project the company should spend its own money on.
Payroll accounting records what employees are paid, which has nothing to do with comparing returns on equipment projects.

q.s: Noah earns $150 a month from his part-time job and sets a goal to save $5,000 for a car within six months. Which characteristic of a SMART goal does Noah's goal lack?
q.r: Attainable. SMART goals are specific, measurable, attainable, realistic, and time-bound. Even if Noah saved every dollar he earned, he would have only $900 after six months, so his goal cannot be reached and is not attainable. The goal is specific because it names the purpose, measurable because it states $5,000, and time-bound because it sets a six-month deadline.
w: Noah's goal is specific because it names exactly what he is saving for, a car, and how much he needs.
Noah's goal is measurable because it sets a clear dollar amount, $5,000, that he can track his progress against.
Noah's goal is time-bound because it has a six-month deadline, so a time frame is not what is missing.

q.s: Elena is saving for a spring-break trip, but at the mall she often buys snacks and accessories that she had not planned to purchase. Which obstacle is keeping Elena from reaching her financial goal?
q.r: Impulse spending. Impulse spending is buying items on the spur of the moment without planning, and it is a common obstacle that pulls money away from financial goals such as savings. Elena could limit it by setting a spending limit or waiting before buying. Inflation is a general rise in prices, credit history relates to borrowing, and tax liability is the tax a person owes; none is causing Elena's problem.
w: Inflation is a general rise in prices, but Elena's problem is her own unplanned buying at the mall, not prices going up.
Credit history relates to how someone has handled borrowing, and nothing in the question says Elena is borrowing money.
Tax liability is the tax a person owes, which is not what is pulling money away from Elena's trip savings.

q.pt: Explain the time value of money
q.s: Ruth deposits $2,500 in a savings account that earns 4% interest compounded annually. If she makes no withdrawals or additional deposits, how much will be in the account at the end of three years?
q.r: $2,812.16. With compound interest, each year's interest is added to the balance and then earns interest itself. The future value is $2,500 x (1.04)^3 = $2,500 x 1.124864 = $2,812.16. $2,800.00 uses simple interest, which ignores interest earned on interest. $2,600.00 is the balance after only one year, and $2,924.65 is the balance after four years.
w: $2,600.00 is the balance after only one year of interest, but Ruth leaves her money in the account for three years.
$2,800.00 uses simple interest, which ignores the interest earned on interest that compounding adds each year.
$2,924.65 is what the account would hold after four years of compounding, one year longer than the question asks about.

q.pt: Explain the time value of money
q.s: Carlos can receive a $5,000 payment today or the same $5,000 one year from now. According to the time value of money, why is the payment today worth more?
o: The later payment will grow with interest before it arrives
Money received in the future has more purchasing power
A future payment is less likely to go unpaid
Money received today can be invested to earn interest
q.r: Money received today can be invested to earn interest. The time value of money is the principle that a dollar today is worth more than a dollar in the future, because money available now can be saved or invested and grow. If Carlos invests $5,000 today, he will have more than $5,000 a year from now; waiting means giving up that interest, an opportunity cost. The later payment stays at $5,000 and does not grow, inflation usually lowers future purchasing power, and a future payment carries more risk of going unpaid, not less.
w: The later payment stays exactly $5,000 and does not grow while Carlos waits; only money in hand now can be invested to earn interest.
Future money usually has less purchasing power, not more, because rising prices mean the same $5,000 will buy less next year.
A promised future payment carries more risk of not being paid, not less, which is another reason money in hand today is worth more.

q.s: A small business has cash of $12,400, accounts receivable of $8,750, inventory of $21,300, equipment of $36,000, accounts payable of $9,600, and a note payable of $15,000. What are the business's total assets?
q.r: $78,450. Assets are the things of value a business owns or is owed, including cash, accounts receivable, inventory, and equipment: $12,400 + $8,750 + $21,300 + $36,000 = $78,450. Accounts payable and notes payable are liabilities, so they are not included. $53,850 subtracts the liabilities, $103,050 adds them, and $42,450 leaves out the equipment, which is a fixed asset.
w: $42,450 leaves out the $36,000 of equipment, which is a fixed asset and must be included in total assets.
$53,850 subtracts the accounts payable and note payable, but liabilities are not taken out when adding up total assets.
$103,050 adds in the accounts payable and note payable, which are liabilities the business owes, not assets it owns.

q.s: A landscaping business records revenue on the day it bills a customer for completed work, even though the customer will not pay until next month. The business is using __________ accounting.
q.r: Accrual-basis. Under accrual-basis accounting, revenue is recorded when it is earned and expenses are recorded when they are incurred, regardless of when cash actually changes hands. Cash-basis accounting records revenue only when payment is received and expenses only when they are paid. Managerial accounting prepares information for internal decision making, and tax accounting prepares information to meet tax laws; neither describes when revenue is recorded.
w: Cash-basis accounting records revenue only when payment is received, but this business records it when it bills, before any cash arrives.
Managerial accounting prepares information for managers' internal decisions; it does not describe the rule for when revenue gets recorded.
Tax accounting focuses on following tax laws, not on the rule of recording revenue when it is earned rather than when cash comes in.

q.s: Ming finds a late payment on her credit report for a credit card that she has always paid on time. What should Ming do first?
o: Close all of her existing credit card accounts
Dispute the error with the credit bureau
Wait several years for the item to drop off
Apply for a new credit card to raise her score
q.r: Dispute the error with the credit bureau. Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, consumers have the right to dispute inaccurate information, and the credit bureau must investigate and correct or remove errors. Ming should explain the error in writing and include copies of proof, such as payment records. Closing accounts or opening new ones does not fix the error, and waiting lets inaccurate information keep hurting her credit.
w: Closing all her credit cards does not remove the wrong late payment and can even hurt her credit by raising the share of available credit she uses.
Waiting years lets the inaccurate late payment keep hurting her credit, when she has the right to have the error fixed now.
Applying for a new card does nothing to correct the error, and the new application can actually lower her score a little.

q.s: Why should consumers review their credit reports regularly?
o: To make sure the information lenders see is accurate
To increase the interest rates on their savings
To remove late payments that are reported accurately
To get their credit limits raised automatically
q.r: To make sure the information lenders see is accurate. Lenders, landlords, insurers, and some employers use credit reports to judge a person's financial responsibility, so errors can lead to denials or higher interest rates. Consumers are responsible for monitoring their own reports and can get free copies from the three major credit bureaus. Reviewing reports does not change savings rates, cannot remove accurate negative items, and does not raise credit limits.
w: Credit reports show borrowing and payment history, and checking them has no effect on the interest rate a savings account pays.
Late payments that are reported correctly generally stay on a credit report, so reviewing it can only fix mistakes, not erase true information.
Lenders decide credit limits based on their own review, and reading your credit report does not trigger an automatic increase.

q.pt: Discuss considerations in selecting a financial-services provider
q.s: Before hiring an investment advisor, which question is most important for Tyler to ask?
o: Which stocks have you bought for yourself this year?
How many of your clients live in my neighborhood?
Which investments will earn me the highest return?
How are you paid, and what fees will I be charged?
q.r: How are you paid, and what fees will I be charged? An advisor's fees and commissions reduce the investor's returns, and the way an advisor is paid can create conflicts of interest. Tyler should also check the advisor's qualifications and background, such as through FINRA BrokerCheck. The advisor's personal stock picks and clients' locations do not show whether the advisor fits Tyler's needs, and no advisor can know in advance which investments will earn the highest return.
w: The advisor's personal stock picks do not show whether the advisor fits Tyler's needs or what working together will cost him.
Where other clients live tells Tyler nothing about the advisor's costs, qualifications, or possible conflicts of interest.
No advisor can know in advance which investments will earn the highest return, so this question cannot get a reliable answer.

q.pt: Discuss considerations in selecting a financial-services provider
q.s: Which type of financial advisor is paid only by the client and does not earn commissions on the investment products the client buys?
q.r: Fee-only advisor. A fee-only advisor is paid directly by the client through an hourly rate, a flat fee, or a percentage of assets managed, so the advisor does not earn more by selling particular products. This reduces conflicts of interest. A commission-based advisor and a full-service broker earn money from the products or trades they sell, and an insurance agent typically earns commissions on policies sold.
w: A commission-based advisor earns money from the products the client buys, which is exactly what the question says this advisor does not do.
A full-service broker typically earns commissions or fees on trades and products sold, so the broker is not paid only by the client.
An insurance agent usually earns commissions on the policies sold, so this person is not paid only directly by the client.

q.s: Lena wants to lower the monthly premium she pays for her health insurance policy. Which action would most likely help her do this?
o: Choose a plan with a higher deductible
Choose a plan with a lower out-of-pocket maximum
Add more family members to the policy
Choose a plan with lower copayments
q.r: Choose a plan with a higher deductible. A deductible is the amount the insured pays for covered services before the insurance company begins paying. When the policyholder agrees to pay more of the cost through a higher deductible, the insurer takes on less risk and charges a lower premium. A lower out-of-pocket maximum, more family members, or lower copayments all increase the costs the insurer expects to pay, which raises the premium.
w: A lower out-of-pocket maximum means the insurer pays more of Lena's costs, which raises the premium instead of lowering it.
Adding family members means the insurer covers more people and expects to pay more claims, so the premium would go up.
Lower copayments shift more of each visit's cost to the insurer, which usually leads to a higher premium, not a lower one.

q.s: Each time Rosa visits her doctor, she pays a flat $25, and her health plan pays the rest of the covered cost of the visit. The $25 Rosa pays is a
q.r: Copayment. A copayment, or copay, is a fixed dollar amount the insured person pays for a covered service, such as a doctor visit or prescription, at the time of care. A premium is the regular payment made to keep the insurance policy in force. A deductible is the amount the insured must pay for covered care each year before the insurer starts paying, and a claim is a request for the insurer to pay for a loss.
w: A premium is the regular payment made to keep the insurance policy active, not the flat amount paid at each doctor visit.
A deductible is the total a person pays each year before insurance starts covering costs, not a set $25 charge every visit.
A claim is a request asking the insurer to pay for a loss or service, not the amount Rosa herself pays at the visit.

q.s: Which of the following practices best helps a person protect against identity theft:
o: Carrying a Social Security card every day
Using one password for every online account
Shredding old papers that show account numbers
Posting a full birth date on social media
q.r: Shredding old papers that show account numbers. Identity thieves often search trash for bank statements, credit offers, and bills that contain personal information. Shredding these documents removes that source of information. Carrying a Social Security card every day risks losing it, using one password everywhere lets a single breach expose every account, and posting a full birth date gives thieves information used to verify identity.
w: Carrying a Social Security card every day makes it more likely to be lost or stolen, which increases the risk of identity theft.
Using one password for every account means a single breach exposes all of them, which weakens protection against identity theft.
Posting a full birth date online gives thieves information often used to verify identity, which increases the risk rather than reducing it.

q.s: After learning that his personal data was exposed in a company's data breach, Omar wants to keep criminals from opening new credit accounts in his name. Which action would be most effective?
o: Request higher credit limits on his existing credit cards
Switch his checking account to a different bank branch
Stop using his debit card for in-store purchases
Freeze his credit at each major credit bureau
q.r: Freeze his credit at each major credit bureau. A security freeze, or credit freeze, blocks lenders from viewing a person's credit report, so new accounts generally cannot be opened in that person's name until the freeze is lifted. Freezes are free and must be placed separately with Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion. Raising credit limits increases potential losses, and changing branches or avoiding a debit card does not stop new accounts from being opened.
w: Raising limits on his current cards would only increase how much a thief could charge and would not stop new accounts from being opened.
Moving to a different branch keeps the same bank and does nothing to stop criminals from using his stolen data to open new credit elsewhere.
Avoiding his debit card in stores might protect that one card, but it does not stop thieves from opening new accounts in his name.

q.pt: Describe sources of income and compensation
q.s: Which of the following is an example of unearned income:
o: Tips received as a restaurant server
Interest earned on a savings account
Wages paid for working at a store
q.r: Interest earned on a savings account. Unearned income is money received from sources other than working, such as interest, dividends, rent from property, and certain government benefits. Earned income is money received in exchange for work performed. Tips, commissions, and hourly wages are all forms of earned income because the person receives them for providing labor or services.
w: Tips are paid to a server for providing service, so they count as earned income rather than unearned income.
Commission is paid for the work of selling cars, which makes it earned income, not income received without working.
Wages are paid in exchange for working at the store, so they are earned income, the opposite of unearned income.

q.s: When an investor buys a corporate bond, the investor is
o: lending money to the company in exchange for interest.
buying partial ownership of the company and its profits.
insuring the company against losses in exchange for fees.
guaranteeing the company's other debts if it defaults.
q.r: Lending money to the company in exchange for interest. A bond is a lending investment: the bondholder lends money to a corporation or government, which promises to pay interest and repay the principal on the maturity date. Buying stock, not bonds, makes an investor a part-owner who shares in profits. Bondholders do not insure the company against losses or guarantee its other debts.
w: Buying partial ownership and a share of profits describes buying stock, while a bond is a loan to the company.
Bondholders do not insure the company or collect fees for covering losses; they lend money and receive interest.
Buying a bond does not make an investor responsible for the company's other debts; the bondholder is a lender, not a guarantor.

q.s: Grace opens an account at a not-for-profit financial institution that is owned by its members, who share a common bond such as their employer or community. Grace has joined a
q.r: Credit union. A credit union is a member-owned, not-for-profit financial institution that serves people who share a common bond, such as an employer, school, or community. Because profits are returned to members, credit unions often offer lower loan rates and fewer fees. Commercial banks are owned by stockholders and operate for profit, brokerage firms buy and sell securities, and finance companies make loans but do not take deposits.
w: A commercial bank is owned by stockholders and run for profit, while the institution Grace joined is not-for-profit and owned by its members.
A brokerage firm buys and sells securities for investors, not a member-owned institution where people with a common bond keep accounts.
A finance company makes loans, but it is not a member-owned, not-for-profit institution based on a common bond like an employer.

q.pt: Explain the need to save and invest
q.s: Devon's employer adds 50 cents to his 401(k) retirement account for every dollar he contributes, up to 6% of his pay. What is the main advantage of contributing to this plan?
o: He receives extra money through matching contributions
His account will earn a fixed rate of interest
He can withdraw his money before retirement without penalty
His investments are insured against loss by the FDIC
q.r: He receives extra money through matching contributions. An employer match adds free money to an employee's retirement savings, and that money can grow through compounding along with the employee's own contributions. Not contributing enough to earn the full match is like turning down part of one's pay. 401(k) investments rise and fall with the market rather than earning a fixed rate, early withdrawals usually bring taxes and penalties, and the FDIC insures bank deposits, not investments.
w: A 401(k) is usually invested in funds that rise and fall with the market, so it does not guarantee a fixed rate of interest.
Withdrawing 401(k) money before retirement age usually brings taxes and penalties, so penalty-free early access is not its advantage.
The FDIC insures bank deposits, not investments, so the money in Devon's 401(k) is not protected against market losses.

q.pt: Discuss the nature of retirement planning
q.s: Harold's employer promises to pay him a specific monthly amount for life after he retires, based on his salary and years of service. Harold is covered by a __________ plan.
q.r: Defined-benefit. A defined-benefit plan, often called a pension, promises retirees a set payout that is usually based on salary and years of service, and the employer bears the investment risk. In a defined-contribution plan, such as a 401(k), the amount put in is set, but the final payout depends on investment results. An individual retirement account is opened by the worker, and profit-sharing ties employer contributions to company profits.
w: A defined-contribution plan, such as a 401(k), sets how much goes in, but its payout depends on investments rather than a promised monthly amount.
An individual retirement account is opened and funded by the worker, not a lifetime monthly payment promised by Harold's employer.
Profit-sharing ties employer contributions to company profits, so it does not guarantee Harold a set monthly amount based on salary and service.

q.s: Which strategy would best help Yasmin avoid late fees on her monthly bills?
o: Pay each bill only after receiving a past-due notice
Pay the bill with the smallest balance first each month
Keep a payment calendar listing each bill's due date
Wait until the last day of the month to pay every bill
q.r: Keep a payment calendar listing each bill's due date. A payment schedule or calendar, along with reminders or automatic payments, helps a person pay each bill on time. Paying on time avoids late fees and extra interest and protects a person's credit history. Waiting for past-due notices guarantees late payments, paying the smallest balance first ignores due dates, and paying everything at month's end will miss bills due earlier.
w: Paying only after a past-due notice arrives means the bill is already late, so Yasmin would still be charged late fees.
Paying the smallest balance first ignores due dates, so a larger bill due earlier in the month could still be paid late.
Waiting until the last day of the month to pay everything will miss any bills that are due earlier in the month.

q.s: Jasmine borrows $6,000 to buy a motorcycle and agrees to repay the loan in 24 monthly payments of $268.50. What is the total finance charge for the loan?
q.r: $444.00. The finance charge is the total cost of credit, or the amount paid above the amount borrowed. Total payments are 24 x $268.50 = $6,444.00, and $6,444.00 - $6,000.00 = $444.00. $6,444.00 is the total amount repaid, not the cost of borrowing, and $268.50 is a single monthly payment. $644.00 results from a subtraction error.
w: $268.50 is just one monthly payment; the finance charge is the total of all 24 payments minus the $6,000 borrowed.
$644.00 comes from a subtraction slip; 24 x $268.50 = $6,444.00, and taking away the $6,000 borrowed leaves $444.00.
$6,444.00 is the total Jasmine repays over 24 months, but the finance charge is only the part above the $6,000 that was borrowed.

q.pt: Explain legal responsibilities associated with consumer financial products and services
q.s: Under the Truth in Lending Act, lenders must
o: approve every applicant who has a steady job.
charge the same interest rate to every borrower.
forgive loans for borrowers who lose their jobs.
disclose credit costs before the borrower signs.
q.r: Disclose credit costs before the borrower signs. The Truth in Lending Act requires lenders to clearly state the key terms of credit, including the annual percentage rate (APR), the finance charge, and the total amount to be repaid, so consumers can compare offers. Borrowers in turn are legally responsible for repaying as agreed. The law does not require lenders to approve every applicant, charge everyone the same rate, or forgive debts.
w: The Truth in Lending Act is about disclosing credit terms, and it does not force lenders to approve every applicant with a steady job.
Lenders may charge different rates based on risk; the Truth in Lending Act only requires them to clearly disclose the costs they charge.
The Truth in Lending Act does not forgive loans when borrowers lose jobs; borrowers remain responsible for repaying as agreed.

q.s: Which of the following is an example of a variable expense in a personal budget:
q.r: Groceries. Variable expenses are costs that change from month to month, such as groceries, gasoline, clothing, and entertainment, and they are often the easiest place to cut spending in a budget. Fixed expenses stay the same each period. Monthly rent, a car loan payment, and a set-price streaming subscription are fixed expenses because the amount owed does not change from month to month.
w: Monthly rent is usually the same amount each month, which makes it a fixed expense rather than one that changes from month to month.
A car loan payment is a set amount due each month, so it is a fixed expense rather than a variable one.
A streaming subscription at a set price costs the same every month, which makes it a fixed expense in a personal budget.

q.pt: Demonstrate the wise use of credit
q.s: Ana uses her credit card for planned monthly purchases and pays the full statement balance by the due date every month. What is the primary benefit of this practice?
o: She avoids interest and builds good credit
Her credit limit increases each time she pays
She can skip reviewing her monthly statements
Her card issuer will waive her annual fee
q.r: She avoids interest and builds good credit. When a cardholder pays the full balance by the due date, most cards charge no interest on purchases, so the card works like a free short-term loan. On-time payments and low balances also build a positive credit history. Paying in full does not raise a credit limit with each payment or lead the issuer to waive annual fees, and cardholders should still check statements for errors.
w: Paying in full each month does not automatically raise a credit limit; issuers decide limits separately, and the main benefit is avoiding interest.
Ana should still review her statements to catch errors or fraud, because paying in full does not protect her from mistakes on the bill.
Card issuers do not usually waive annual fees just because a cardholder pays in full; Ana's main benefit is avoiding interest and building credit.

q.s: Ben stops making payments on his auto loan, and the car was pledged as collateral when he took out the loan. What can the lender most likely do?
o: Repossess the car to recover the money owed
Cancel the remaining balance of the loan
Lower the loan's interest rate to zero
Transfer the debt to Ben's employer
q.r: Repossess the car to recover the money owed. A secured loan is backed by collateral, which is property the lender may take if the borrower defaults. With an auto loan, the car itself is the collateral, so the lender can repossess and sell it, and Ben may still owe any remaining balance. Default does not cancel the debt or lower the interest rate, and an employer is not responsible for an employee's loan.
w: Stopping payments does not erase Ben's debt; because the car is collateral, the lender can take it, and Ben may still owe any remaining balance.
A lender has no reason to cut the interest rate to zero when a borrower stops paying; default usually brings penalties, not better terms.
Ben's employer is not responsible for his personal loan, so the lender cannot simply move the debt to the employer.

q.s: Kendra has $1,850 in checking, $4,200 in savings, a car worth $9,500, and personal property worth $3,100. She owes $6,300 on her car loan and $740 on a credit card. What is Kendra's net worth?
q.r: $11,610. Net worth is total assets minus total liabilities. Kendra's assets are $1,850 + $4,200 + $9,500 + $3,100 = $18,650, and her liabilities are $6,300 + $740 = $7,040, so her net worth is $18,650 - $7,040 = $11,610. $18,650 is total assets only, $7,040 is total liabilities only, and $25,690 incorrectly adds liabilities to assets.
w: $7,040 is Kendra's total liabilities ($6,300 + $740); net worth subtracts that amount from her total assets.
$18,650 is Kendra's total assets; it forgets to subtract the $7,040 she owes on her car loan and credit card.
$25,690 adds the $7,040 in debts to the $18,650 in assets, but debts reduce net worth, so they must be subtracted.

q.pt: Explain the nature of estate planning
q.s: In her will, Margaret names her son to manage her estate, pay her final debts, and distribute her property after her death. Her son is the estate's
q.r: Executor. An executor is the person named in a will to carry out its instructions, which includes gathering the deceased person's assets, paying debts and taxes, and distributing property as the will directs. A beneficiary is a person who receives property from the estate. A guardian is appointed to care for minor children or others who cannot care for themselves, and a notary witnesses signatures on legal documents.
w: A beneficiary receives property from an estate, but Margaret's son is named to manage the estate, pay debts and hand out property to others.
A guardian is appointed to care for minor children or others who cannot care for themselves, not to settle debts and distribute an estate.
A notary witnesses signatures on legal documents but has no role in paying Margaret's final debts or distributing her property.

q.s: Simone is thinking about buying a $900 laptop. What is the most responsible first step she should take?
o: Determine how the purchase fits within her budget
Open a store credit card to receive a discount
Choose the model that most of her friends own
Buy it today before the price can increase
q.r: Determine how the purchase fits within her budget. Responsible financial decisions start by weighing a purchase against income, expenses, savings goals, and other priorities. Once Simone knows what she can afford, she can compare models, prices, and reviews. Opening a store card for a discount can lead to high-interest debt, following friends ignores her own needs, and rushing to buy skips the planning that prevents regret.
w: Opening a store credit card for a discount can lead to high-interest debt, and it skips checking whether Simone can afford the laptop at all.
Choosing the model her friends own ignores Simone's own needs and budget, which should come first in a responsible decision.
Buying today to beat a possible price increase is a rushed decision that skips checking whether the $900 laptop fits her budget.

q.s: Each January, Ruby's employer sends her a form that shows her total wages for the year and the taxes withheld, which she uses to complete her federal income tax return. This form is a
q.r: Form W-2. Employers must give each employee a Form W-2, the Wage and Tax Statement, showing the year's wages and the federal, state, Social Security, and Medicare taxes withheld. Employees use it to prepare their tax returns. Form W-4 is completed by the employee to tell the employer how much tax to withhold, Form 1099 reports other income such as freelance pay or interest, and Form 1040 is the individual income tax return itself.
w: Form W-4 is filled out by the employee to tell the employer how much tax to withhold, not sent by the employer to report the year's wages.
Form 1099 reports income that is not regular wages, such as freelance pay or interest, while Ruby's form shows wages from her employer.
Form 1040 is the tax return Ruby completes herself; the form her employer sends is the wage statement she uses to fill it out.

q.s: Which practice would best help Luis manage his online banking account securely?
o: Log in over free public Wi-Fi networks
Save his password in an unlocked phone note
Click email links that ask him to verify the account
Turn on multifactor authentication and account alerts
q.r: Turn on multifactor authentication and account alerts. Multifactor authentication requires a second proof of identity, such as a code sent to a phone, so a stolen password alone cannot open the account. Alerts notify Luis of transactions right away so he can spot fraud quickly. Public Wi-Fi can expose login information, an unprotected password note is easy to find, and email links asking for account verification are common phishing scams.
w: Free public Wi-Fi is often unsecured, so logging in to a bank account there could let others capture Luis's login information.
A password saved in an unlocked phone note can be read by anyone who picks up the phone, which weakens the account's security.
Email links asking you to verify an account are a common phishing trick to steal login details, so clicking them puts the account at risk.

q.pt: Discuss options for financing a college education
q.s: When paying for college, which source of funds should a student generally use before taking out loans because it does not have to be repaid?
q.r: Grants and scholarships. Grants are usually based on financial need and scholarships on merit or other criteria, but both are gift aid that does not have to be repaid. Students apply for federal grants by completing the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA). Private student loans, credit cards, and parent loans are all forms of borrowing that must be repaid with interest, so they should be used only after free aid.
w: Private student loans are borrowed money that must be repaid with interest, so they should come after free aid, not before it.
Credit cards are a form of borrowing, often with high interest, so they are a costly way to pay for college rather than money that is free.
Parent loans are still loans that must be repaid with interest, so they are not the free aid a student should use first.

q.pt: Explain the nature of balance sheets
q.s: Which of the following is the basic accounting equation on which the balance sheet is based:
q.r: Assets = Liabilities + Owner's equity. The balance sheet is built on the accounting equation, which shows that everything a business owns is financed either by creditors (liabilities) or by owners (owner's equity). The two sides must always be equal, which is why the statement is said to balance. Revenues minus expenses determines net income on the income statement, and the other options misplace the elements of the equation.
w: Revenues minus expenses is how net income is figured on the income statement; the balance sheet compares what a business owns with who financed it.
This version puts owner's equity on the wrong side; liabilities equal assets minus owner's equity, not assets plus owner's equity.
Revenues belong on the income statement, not the balance sheet, so this mixes elements from two different financial statements.

q.pt: Explain the nature of balance sheets
q.s: A lender reviewing a company's balance sheet would learn about the business's
o: revenues and expenses over a period.
financial position on a specific date.
cash receipts and payments over a period.
planned spending for the coming year.
q.r: Financial position on a specific date. A balance sheet lists a business's assets, liabilities, and owner's equity as of one particular day, giving a snapshot of what the company owns and owes. Lenders use it to judge whether the business has enough assets to cover its debts. Revenues and expenses over a period appear on the income statement, cash receipts and payments appear on the cash flow statement, and planned spending appears in a budget.
w: Revenues and expenses over a period are shown on the income statement, while a balance sheet shows what a business owns and owes on one date.
Cash coming in and going out over time is reported on the cash flow statement, not on the balance sheet the lender is reviewing.
Planned spending for the coming year belongs in a budget, while a balance sheet reports the business's current assets, debts, and equity.

q.pt: Describe the nature of income statements
q.s: A retailer's income statement shows net sales of $184,000, cost of goods sold of $112,500, and operating expenses of $49,300. What is the retailer's net income?
q.r: $22,200. On an income statement, gross profit equals net sales minus cost of goods sold: $184,000 - $112,500 = $71,500. Net income equals gross profit minus operating expenses: $71,500 - $49,300 = $22,200. $71,500 is gross profit, not net income. $134,700 subtracts only operating expenses from sales, and $63,200 subtracts operating expenses from cost of goods sold.
w: $63,200 subtracts operating expenses from cost of goods sold, but net income starts with net sales, not cost of goods sold.
$71,500 is gross profit, net sales minus cost of goods sold, and operating expenses still need to be subtracted to reach net income.
$134,700 subtracts only operating expenses from net sales and leaves out the $112,500 cost of goods sold.

q.pt: Describe the nature of income statements
q.s: Why would a bank loan officer review a business's income statements from the past three years before approving a loan?
o: To judge whether profits can cover loan payments
To learn how much cash the business has today
To find the personal assets of the owner
To set the sales tax rate the business charges
q.r: To judge whether profits can cover loan payments. An income statement summarizes revenues and expenses over a period and shows whether the business earned a net income or suffered a net loss. Several years of statements reveal profit trends that indicate the ability to make loan payments. Cash on hand on a given day appears on the balance sheet, owners' personal assets are not shown, and sales tax rates are set by governments.
w: Cash on hand today appears on the balance sheet, while income statements from three years show profit trends over time.
Business income statements report the company's revenues and expenses, not the owner's personal assets.
Sales tax rates are set by governments, so a loan officer would not use income statements to decide them.

q.pt: Describe the nature of cash flow statements
q.s: A cash flow statement groups a business's cash receipts and cash payments into which three categories?
o: Assets, liabilities, and owner's equity accounts
Revenues, expenses, and net income or loss
q.r: Operating, investing, and financing activities. The cash flow statement shows cash coming in and going out during a period. Operating activities involve day-to-day business, investing activities involve buying or selling long-term assets such as equipment, and financing activities involve borrowing, repaying loans, or raising money from owners. Assets, liabilities, and owner's equity make up the balance sheet; revenues, expenses, and net income are income statement items; and fixed and variable costs describe cost behavior.
w: Assets, liabilities, and owner's equity are the parts of a balance sheet, not the categories used to group cash receipts and payments.
Revenues, expenses, and net income or loss belong on the income statement, while the cash flow statement sorts actual cash movements by activity.
Fixed, variable, and semivariable costs describe how costs behave as output changes, not how a cash flow statement groups cash.

q.s: Which of the following is a basic characteristic of budgets:
o: They are prepared after the period ends
They are used mainly to file tax returns
They cover a specific period of time
They are required by federal law
q.r: They cover a specific period of time. A budget is a financial plan that estimates income and expenses for a definite future period, such as a month, quarter, or year. It serves as a target and as a standard for measuring actual performance. Budgets are prepared before the period begins, are planning tools rather than tax filings, and are not required by federal law for private businesses, though managers rely on them to compare actual and budgeted figures.
w: Budgets are plans made before a period starts; comparing results after the period ends is a later step that uses the budget.
Budgets are planning tools for estimating income and expenses, not documents prepared mainly for filing tax returns.
Private businesses are generally not required by federal law to prepare budgets; they use them because budgets help plan and measure performance.

q.s: Eighteen-year-old Ava has no credit history and was turned down for a car loan. Which action would most likely help her qualify for the loan?
o: Apply at several lenders on the same afternoon
List a higher income than she earns on the application
Request a larger loan with a longer repayment term
Ask a creditworthy relative to cosign the loan
q.r: Ask a creditworthy relative to cosign the loan. A cosigner with good credit agrees to repay the loan if the borrower defaults, which lowers the lender's risk and can help an applicant with no credit history get approved. The cosigner becomes legally responsible for the debt. Applying with many lenders does not fix the lack of credit history, overstating income on a loan application is fraud, and a larger loan increases the lender's risk.
w: Applying at many lenders on the same day does not give Ava a credit history, so each lender still sees the same lack of record.
Overstating income on a loan application is fraud, and it can get Ava denied or into legal trouble rather than approved.
A bigger loan with a longer term increases the lender's risk, which makes approval even less likely for someone with no credit history.

q.s: Which of the following people most likely has the greatest need for life insurance:
o: A single college student with no dependents
A retired couple with no debts and grown children
A teenager covered under a parent's health plan
A parent whose income supports two young children
q.r: A parent whose income supports two young children. Determining insurance needs means identifying who would suffer a financial loss and how large that loss could be. Life insurance replaces income for dependents if the insured person dies, so a parent supporting young children has the greatest need. A single student with no dependents, a debt-free retired couple with grown children, and a teenager have few or no people relying on their income.
w: A single college student with no dependents has no one relying on that income, so a death would cause little financial loss to others.
A retired couple with no debts and grown children has few people depending on their income, so their need to replace it is small.
A teenager on a parent's health plan usually has no one depending on their income, which is what life insurance is meant to replace.

q.pt: Discuss the role of ethics in accounting
q.s: An accountant's manager asks her to record next month's sales in this month's report so the company will appear to meet its quarterly goal. What is the ethical action?
o: Record the sales early but add a note in her personal files
Refuse and record the sales in the period they actually occur
Record the sales early because the manager accepts responsibility
Record half of the sales early as a compromise
q.r: Refuse and record the sales in the period they actually occur. Ethics in accounting requires recording and reporting financial information honestly, accurately, and objectively. Moving sales into the wrong period misleads owners, investors, and lenders about the company's true performance. A private note does not correct the misleading report, following a manager's order does not make a dishonest entry acceptable, and recording half the sales early is still misstating results.
w: A note in her personal files does nothing to fix the misleading report that owners, investors and lenders will see.
A manager taking responsibility does not make a false entry honest; the report would still mislead people about the company's real results.
Recording half the sales early still misstates the company's results, so a compromise does not make the dishonest entry ethical.

q.pt: Explain the use of technology in accounting
q.s: What is a major advantage of cloud-based accounting software for a small business?
o: It reduces the need for passwords and access controls
It lets authorized users access current records anywhere
It prevents users from entering incorrect transactions
It lowers the tax rate the business must pay
q.r: It lets authorized users access current records anywhere. Cloud-based accounting software stores financial data online, updates it automatically, and lets owners, employees, and accountants work with the same up-to-date records wherever they are. It also automates tasks such as invoicing and payroll. Online data actually calls for strong passwords and access controls, transactions still need review because software cannot stop people from entering incorrect amounts, and the software does not change a business's tax rate.
w: Storing financial data online actually makes passwords and access controls more important, since records can be reached from many places.
Cloud software can automate some tasks, but it cannot stop people from typing incorrect amounts, so transactions still need to be reviewed.
The business's tax rate is set by tax law, and where its accounting software stores data does not change what it owes.

q.s: Which statement accurately describes the Sarbanes-Oxley Act?
o: It requires small businesses to use cash-basis accounting
It sets the federal minimum wage for accounting employees
It requires public-company CEOs to certify financial reports
It limits the interest rates that banks may charge borrowers
q.r: It requires public-company CEOs to certify financial reports. The Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 was passed after major accounting scandals to increase the accuracy and transparency of corporate financial reporting. It makes chief executives and chief financial officers personally responsible for the accuracy of reports and requires strong internal controls. It does not require cash-basis accounting, set minimum wages, which the Fair Labor Standards Act covers, or cap bank interest rates.
w: Sarbanes-Oxley deals with the accuracy of public companies' financial reports and does not require small businesses to use cash-basis accounting.
Minimum wage is set by the Fair Labor Standards Act, while Sarbanes-Oxley focuses on honest, accurate corporate financial reporting.
Sarbanes-Oxley does not limit bank interest rates; it was passed after accounting scandals to make corporate financial reports more trustworthy.

q.pt: Discuss the role of ethics in finance
q.s: A financial advisor recommends a mutual fund mainly because it pays her the highest commission, even though a lower-cost fund better fits her client's goals. This is an example of a
q.r: Conflict of interest. A conflict of interest occurs when a person's own interests, such as earning a larger commission, compete with the duty to act in a client's best interest. Ethical financial professionals disclose and avoid such conflicts. Diversification is spreading investments to reduce risk, fiduciary duty is the obligation to put the client first, which the advisor is failing to meet, and risk tolerance is how much risk an investor can accept.
w: Diversification is spreading investments to reduce risk, which has nothing to do with choosing a fund because it pays the advisor more.
Fiduciary duty is the obligation to put the client first, which is exactly what this advisor fails to do by chasing a higher commission.
Risk tolerance is how much risk an investor can accept, but the problem here is the advisor's personal gain competing with the client's interests.

q.pt: Discuss the role of ethics in finance
q.s: Why is ethical behavior especially important for people who work in finance?
o: Ethical firms pay lower taxes than other firms
Ethics rules allow firms to delay reporting losses
Ethical firms face fewer government regulations
Dishonesty can cause severe losses and destroy trust
q.r: Dishonesty can cause severe losses and destroy trust. Financial professionals handle other people's money and information, so unethical acts such as fraud or misleading advice can wipe out savings, harm businesses, and damage confidence in the entire financial system. Ethical firms do not pay lower taxes, ethical behavior requires reporting losses promptly rather than delaying them, and the same laws and regulators oversee every financial firm.
w: Taxes are set by law, not by how ethical a firm is, so acting ethically does not earn a business a lower tax bill.
Ethical behavior calls for reporting losses honestly and promptly; hiding or delaying them is the kind of conduct ethics rules forbid.
Ethical and unethical financial firms answer to the same laws and regulators, so good behavior does not reduce the rules a firm must follow.

q.s: Which federal agency enforces laws that require companies selling stock to the public to disclose accurate information about their finances and risks?
q.r: Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). The SEC regulates the securities markets and enforces federal securities laws, which require public companies to disclose truthful financial information and investment risks so investors can make informed decisions. It also prosecutes fraud such as insider trading. The FTC protects consumers from unfair and deceptive business practices, OSHA enforces workplace safety rules, and the EEOC enforces laws against employment discrimination.
w: The FTC protects consumers from unfair and deceptive business practices, but rules on disclosing finances to stock buyers are enforced by a different agency.
OSHA enforces workplace safety rules, which have nothing to do with companies sharing accurate financial information with people who buy their stock.
The EEOC enforces laws against job discrimination, not laws requiring companies to disclose their finances and risks to investors.

q.s: Malik's supervisor asks him to research shipping options for the company's new product line. What should Malik do first?
o: Search the internet for every article about shipping
Write a summary of his recommendation
Ask coworkers which carrier they prefer
Determine exactly what information he needs and why
q.r: Determine exactly what information he needs and why. Assessing information needs is the first step in using information effectively. By deciding exactly what he needs to know, how much detail is required, and how the information will be used, Malik can focus his search and avoid wasting time on irrelevant material. Searching broadly, writing a recommendation, or collecting coworkers' preferences should come later, if at all, once his needs are defined.
w: Searching for every article on shipping without a clear goal would bury Malik in material he may not need; he must first define what he is looking for.
Writing a recommendation is one of the last steps, since Malik cannot recommend a shipping option before he knows what information he needs and has gathered it.
Coworkers' carrier preferences might be useful later, but opinions are not a starting point when Malik has not yet decided what information the task requires.

q.s: Hana wants her web search to return only pages that contain the exact phrase customer loyalty program. What should she do?
o: Enclose the phrase in quotation marks
Type the phrase in all capital letters
Place the word OR between each word
Put a minus sign in front of each word
q.r: Enclose the phrase in quotation marks. Most search engines treat words inside quotation marks as an exact phrase, returning only pages in which the words appear together and in that order. This saves time by eliminating many unrelated results. Search engines generally ignore capitalization. Placing OR between the words broadens the search, and a minus sign excludes a word from the results.
w: Search engines generally ignore capitalization, so typing the phrase in all capitals will not limit results to the exact phrase.
Placing OR between the words broadens the search to pages with any one of the words, the opposite of finding the exact phrase.
A minus sign in front of a word excludes that word from results, so this would remove the very words Hana wants to find.

q.s: Gwen needs last quarter's sales figures for her company's western region to finish a report today. Where can she most efficiently obtain this information?
q.r: The company's intranet. An intranet is a private network that only a company's employees can access. Businesses use intranets to share internal information such as sales reports, policies, and forms, so it is the quickest place to find the company's own sales data. A public search engine, a business magazine, and a government website provide outside information and would not contain the company's internal sales figures.
w: A public search engine finds information posted on the open internet, but a company's own regional sales figures are private and would not show up there.
A national business magazine reports on industries and other companies, so it would not contain Gwen's company's internal sales numbers for last quarter.
Government statistics websites offer broad data about the economy and industries, not one company's private sales results for its western region.

q.pt: Evaluate quality and source of information
q.s: Danielle needs current, reliable information about sales trends in the electric-vehicle market. Which of the following sources should she use:
o: A blog post written five years ago by a car enthusiast
An advertisement from a dealer claiming record sales
An anonymous comment posted on a social media forum
A current report from a respected research firm
q.r: A current report from a respected research firm. Reliable information comes from an expert, reputable source and is current enough for the purpose. A report published this year by an established research firm meets both tests. The old blog post is outdated and written by a nonexpert. A dealer's advertisement is biased because it is meant to sell cars. An anonymous comment provides no way to judge the author's expertise.
w: A five-year-old blog post by a hobbyist fails both tests Danielle needs: it is out of date for a fast-changing market and is not written by an expert.
A dealer's ad is meant to sell cars, so its claims of record sales are likely biased rather than an objective picture of market trends.
An anonymous comment gives Danielle no way to check who wrote it or whether that person knows anything about electric-vehicle sales.

q.pt: Evaluate quality and source of information
q.s: A study praising the health benefits of a sports drink was paid for by the company that makes the drink. When evaluating the study, a reader should be most concerned about the information's
q.r: Objectivity. Objectivity refers to whether information is presented fairly and without bias. When the organization that funds a study benefits from its results, the findings may be slanted, so the reader should verify them with independent sources. Timeliness concerns how current the information is, and nothing suggests the study is outdated. A study's format and length do not indicate whether it is biased.
w: Timeliness is about how current information is, and nothing in the question suggests the study is outdated; the worry is who paid for it.
Format is how the information is presented, which says nothing about whether the drink company's funding slanted the results.
A study's length does not reveal whether it is biased, and the concern here is that the company paying for it benefits from its findings.

q.pt: Evaluate quality and source of information
q.s: Carlos found some surprising industry statistics on a little-known website. What is the best way for him to check whether the statistics are accurate?
o: Accept them if the website has a professional design
Count how many times the page has been shared
Use them if they support the point he wants to make
Compare them with other reputable sources
q.r: Compare them with other reputable sources. Cross-checking information against several reputable sources is a key way to evaluate its accuracy. If respected sources report similar figures, Carlos can be more confident that the statistics are correct. A professional-looking design does not guarantee accuracy, and popularity on social media does not make information true. Using information only because it supports his opinion would introduce bias.
w: A professional-looking website can still contain false numbers, since good design shows effort on appearance, not accuracy.
Many shares only show that information is popular, and inaccurate statistics can spread widely online.
Using statistics just because they back up his point would be biased and does nothing to show whether the numbers are true.

q.pt: Evaluate quality and source of information
q.s: When evaluating a source, a researcher who asks, "When was this published, and has it been updated?" is judging the information's
q.r: Timeliness. Timeliness, or currency, describes how up to date information is. Information about fast-changing topics, such as technology or market conditions, can quickly become outdated, so researchers check publication and revision dates. Authority refers to the expertise of the author or publisher. Objectivity refers to freedom from bias. Relevance refers to how closely the information relates to the researcher's needs.
w: Authority is about the expertise of the author or publisher, while the researcher is asking when the information was published and updated.
Objectivity is about whether information is free from bias, not about how recent or up to date it is.
Relevance is about how closely information fits the researcher's needs, while publication and update dates measure how current it is.

q.pt: Draw conclusions based on information analysis
q.s: A café's sales records show that 70% of its customers visit between 7:00 and 9:00 a.m. and only 5% visit after 3:00 p.m. Which of the following conclusions is best supported by this information:
o: Most of the café's business occurs in the early morning
Customers dislike the items on the afternoon menu
The café should raise its prices in the morning
Afternoon customers spend more money per visit
q.r: Most of the café's business occurs in the early morning. A valid conclusion is one that is directly supported by the facts that were analyzed. The data clearly show when customers visit, so the café can conclude that most of its business takes place in the early morning. The data say nothing about why customers avoid the afternoon, how they feel about prices, or how much each customer spends, so the other conclusions are not supported.
w: The data show when customers visit, not how they feel about the food, so nothing supports the claim that they dislike the afternoon menu.
Raising morning prices is a business decision the café might consider, but visit-time data alone does not show that higher prices would work.
The figures count visits by time of day and say nothing about how much each customer spends, so this conclusion goes beyond the data.

q.pt: Apply information to accomplish a task
q.s: Mateo restates the ideas of a long industry article in his own words, keeping about the same level of detail, and credits the original author. Mateo is
q.r: Paraphrasing. Paraphrasing is restating someone else's ideas in your own words while keeping roughly the same length and detail. Because Mateo credits the author, he is using the information properly. Summarizing would condense the article into only its main points. Quoting means repeating the author's exact words inside quotation marks. Plagiarizing is presenting another person's work or ideas as your own without giving credit.
w: Summarizing shrinks a source down to its main points, but Mateo keeps about the same level of detail as the original article.
Quoting means repeating the author's exact words inside quotation marks, while Mateo is putting the ideas into his own words.
Plagiarizing is passing off someone else's ideas as your own, but Mateo gives credit to the original author, so he is using the source honestly.

q.s: Ashford Supply cannot open important files it saved 15 years ago because it no longer owns equipment that can read the disks they were stored on. This situation shows that storage media can become
q.r: Obsolete. Storage technology changes rapidly, and media such as floppy disks or older file formats may no longer be supported by current equipment and software. To keep stored information usable, businesses should periodically transfer important records to current media and formats. Encrypted files are coded for security, not unreadable because of age. Overloaded and duplicated do not describe media that can no longer be read.
w: Encryption scrambles data on purpose to keep it secure, but Ashford's problem is that no one has the old equipment needed to read the disks.
Overloaded suggests a device holding too much data, which does not explain why 15-year-old disks cannot be read on today's equipment.
Duplicated means copies exist, which would actually help preserve files; it does not describe disks that current machines can no longer read.

q.s: What is an advantage of storing business records with a cloud-based service rather than on a single office computer?
o: Authorized employees can reach the records from almost anywhere
The records no longer need to be protected by passwords
The records can be retrieved without an internet connection
Files are automatically sorted into the correct folders
q.r: Authorized employees can reach the records from almost anywhere. Cloud storage keeps information on remote servers that users reach over the internet. Because of this, authorized employees can retrieve records anytime and from almost any location, and a damaged office computer will not destroy the files. However, cloud storage still requires password protection and an internet connection, and users must still organize their files, so the other options are incorrect.
w: Cloud records still need password protection; storing them online actually makes strong passwords more important, not less.
Cloud storage is reached over the internet, so records generally cannot be retrieved without a connection; that is a limitation, not an advantage.
Cloud services store files remotely, but users still have to organize them; the service does not sort files into the right folders by itself.

q.s: When setting up a system to store information for future use, a business should
o: keep documents indefinitely in case they are needed later.
let employees store files wherever they find most convenient.
keep needed information and arrange it in a logical order.
delete project records as soon as the project has ended.
q.r: Keep needed information and arrange it in a logical order. An effective storage system lets users find information quickly when it is needed. Keeping documents indefinitely leads to information overload, making useful records harder to find and adding storage costs. Letting employees store files wherever they like creates disorganization, and deleting project records right away may destroy information needed later for decisions or legal purposes.
w: Keeping every document forever creates clutter that makes useful records harder to find and raises storage costs.
Letting each employee choose where to save files leads to disorganization, so others cannot find information when they need it.
Deleting project records right after a project ends may destroy information needed later for decisions or legal reasons.

q.pt: Discuss the nature of information management
q.s: Burke Plumbing reorganized its customer files so that technicians can find a home's repair history in seconds instead of several minutes. This is an example of how information management helps businesses
q.r: Save time and money. Information management is the process of acquiring, organizing, storing, and using information so that it is available when needed. When employees can quickly locate the information they need, they work more efficiently, which saves time and lowers costs. Faster access to repair histories does not by itself justify higher prices or less advertising, and it allows existing technicians to do more work rather than requiring more technicians.
w: Faster access to repair histories makes technicians more efficient, but it does not by itself give Burke Plumbing a reason to charge customers more.
Reorganizing customer files speeds up service work inside the company; it has no direct link to how much the business spends on advertising.
Finding records in seconds lets the current technicians get more done, which reduces the need for extra workers rather than creating it.

q.pt: Discuss the nature of information management
q.s: A major risk associated with a business's storing large amounts of customer information is that
o: customers will receive faster service than before.
criminals could steal it to commit identity theft.
competitors could legally demand copies of the data.
the information will lose all value after one year.
q.r: Criminals could steal it to commit identity theft. Customer files often contain names, addresses, account numbers, and other personal data that criminals can use to impersonate customers. Because of this privacy and security risk, businesses must protect the information they store. Faster service is a benefit, not a risk. Competitors have no legal right to a firm's customer data, and information does not automatically lose its value after a year.
w: Faster customer service is a benefit of keeping good customer records, not a risk the business has to worry about.
Competitors have no legal right to demand a business's customer data, so this is not a real risk of storing it.
Customer information does not automatically become worthless after a year; much of it stays useful, and stays attractive to thieves, for a long time.

q.pt: Discuss the nature of information management
q.s: An effective information management program ensures that information is
o: stored in printed form for safekeeping.
available to those who need it when needed.
shared equally with all employees in the firm.
copied into several separate filing systems.
q.r: Available to those who need it when needed. The goal of information management is to get the right information to the right people at the right time so they can make decisions and complete tasks. Information may be stored digitally or on paper. Sharing all information with every employee would create privacy problems, and copying it into several separate systems causes duplication, inconsistent records, and information overload.
w: Information can be stored on paper or digitally; an effective program focuses on getting it to the right people, not on printing everything.
Sharing all information with every employee would expose private data to people who do not need it, which creates privacy problems.
Copying information into several separate systems causes duplicates and mismatched records instead of making it easier to use.

q.pt: Explain the role of ethics in information management
q.s: Paolo, a bank employee, looks up his neighbor's account balance in the company database out of curiosity. Paolo's action is unethical because he
o: used the company database during regular work hours.
did not print a copy of the account record.
accessed private information without a business reason.
failed to update the neighbor's mailing address.
q.r: Accessed private information without a business reason. Ethics in information management requires employees to use confidential information only for legitimate work purposes and to respect the privacy of customers. Viewing a customer's account out of curiosity violates that trust, even if nothing is changed or shared. Using the database during work hours is expected, and printing the record or updating the address would not make the access ethical.
w: Using the company database during work hours is expected for a bank employee; the problem is that Paolo had no business reason to look.
Printing a copy of the record would not make the access ethical; Paolo's wrong was viewing private data out of curiosity.
Updating the neighbor's address is not Paolo's task here, and it would not excuse looking up a customer's balance for personal reasons.

q.pt: Explain legal issues associated with information management
