The longer process of integrating new hires into a company, from paperwork and orientation through training, until they become productive members.
The philosophy that a business earns profit by learning what customers want and providing it better than competitors.
The marketing function of gathering, analyzing and using information about customers and markets to make business decisions.
The marketing function of getting products to customers, including selecting distribution channels and handling transportation and storage.
The marketing function of deciding which goods and services to offer and developing, improving, packaging and branding them.
The marketing function of communicating with customers to inform, persuade or remind them about a business's products or image.
Fully concentrating on a speaker in order to understand, respond to and remember the message, rather than simply hearing the words.
Understanding a situation from another person's point of view, including the feelings behind what that person says.
A barrier to listening that comes from within the listener, such as a headache, hunger, worry or daydreaming.
A barrier to listening that comes from the surroundings, such as noise, a ringing phone or an uncomfortable room temperature.
Restating a speaker's message in your own words to confirm that you understood it correctly.
A brief spoken response, such as "I see" or "I understand," that shows a speaker you are paying attention.
Sending messages without words, through facial expressions, eye contact, gestures, posture, tone of voice and use of personal space.
A question asked to remove confusion about a specific point in a message, such as the order in which tasks should be done.
Spoken instructions for completing a task, which the listener must hear, understand and carry out accurately and in order.
Recording key information from a speaker or a reading in brief, organized form so it can be reviewed and used later.
A shortened form of a word, such as "mgmt" for management, used to write notes quickly.
Arranging information in time sequence, from the earliest event or step to the latest.
Using spoken words to share information; it is effective when the receiver understands the message as the sender intended.
Choosing words that express your exact meaning so the listener does not have to guess what you intend.
The pitch, emphasis and emotion in a speaker's voice, which can change the meaning of the same words.
Nonverbal messages sent through posture, gestures, facial expressions and movement, such as crossed arms or a slumped stance.
Reading quickly through titles, headings and key sentences to get the general idea of a text and judge its relevance.
Searching through text quickly to locate a specific fact, name, date or figure without reading everything.
The trustworthiness and expertise of an author or source, which determine whether its information can be relied on.
A general rule or guideline that states what a company expects and guides employees' decisions and actions.
A step-by-step method for carrying out a task or policy, such as the process for requesting petty cash.
The quality of a message expressed in plain, specific language that the receiver understands without confusion.
Carefully checking a final draft for errors in spelling, grammar, punctuation and format before sending or publishing it.
The brief, specific phrase at the top of an email that tells the reader what the message is about.
A business message that shares facts, such as announcements or new policies, that readers are expected to accept readily.
A request for information, products, services or action that states clearly what is needed, why and by when.
A message intended to convince the reader to accept an idea, buy a product or take an action, usually by stressing benefits.
A letter sent after an interview or meeting to thank the reader, restate interest and keep the relationship active.
A letter that accompanies documents being sent, such as contracts or a report, and explains what is enclosed.
A business letter style in which every line, including the date and closing, begins at the left margin with no paragraph indents.
A written message format for communication within an organization, using To, From, Date and Subject headings instead of a salutation.
A circular graph divided into slices that shows how the parts of a whole compare, such as shares of a budget.
A graph that connects data points with a line to show trends or changes over time.
A graph that uses bars of different lengths to compare amounts across categories.
An arrangement of exact figures or words in rows and columns for easy reference and comparison.
A diagram that uses shapes and arrows to show the steps of a process in sequence.
Messages that flow from managers to employees, such as instructions, policies and announcements.
Messages that flow from employees to managers, such as reports, suggestions and concerns.
Messages exchanged between employees or departments at the same level of an organization; also called lateral communication.
The informal, unofficial network through which information and rumors spread among employees, often quickly and inaccurately.
The medium used to send a message, such as a face-to-face conversation, phone call, email, memo or meeting.
Basing judgments and arguments on facts, logic and evidence rather than on personal feelings or bias.
The courteous, businesslike rules for answering, conducting and ending phone calls and for taking accurate messages.
The image others form of a person based on that person's actions, appearance and online activity.
A brief overview at the start of a long report or plan that presents its purpose, key findings and recommendations.
A company's commitment to consistently deliver the experience and benefits customers can expect each time they interact with its products, services or people.
Any point of interaction between a customer and a business, such as advertising, a sales conversation or postsale support, that shapes the customer's view of the brand.
The overall impression the public holds of a business, shaped by its products, communications and the performance of its employees.
An attitude of putting customers' needs first by giving them full attention, looking for ways to help and creating positive experiences.
The interactions between a business and its customers; positive ones are friendly, helpful and respectful and build satisfaction, trust and loyalty.
Customers' ongoing commitment to keep buying from a particular business, which produces repeat business and positive word-of-mouth.
Understanding of the features, uses, benefits and related policies of a business's goods and services, needed to answer customer questions accurately.
A rule or guideline a company sets, such as for returns, exchanges or credit, so decisions are made consistently and support sales and profits.
A customer's expression of dissatisfaction with a product, service or experience, which gives the business a chance to fix the problem and regain trust.
A difficult customer who doubts a salesperson's statements and wants proof, such as facts, demonstrations or guarantees, before believing claims or buying.
A difficult customer who is argumentative, contradicts what the salesperson says and seems to look for reasons to disagree.
A difficult, moody customer whose temper shifts unpredictably and who is easily annoyed, calling for patient, calm and efficient service.
A difficult customer who has trouble making up their mind and needs help narrowing the choices to reach a buying decision.
A difficult customer who acts superior, makes demands and tries to take control of the sales conversation.
A business strategy, supported by software, for identifying, attracting and keeping profitable customers by storing and using customer information to personalize service.
The study of how individuals, businesses and societies use limited resources to satisfy unlimited wants.
The condition of having limited resources but unlimited wants, which forces people and businesses to make choices.
The value of the next-best alternative given up when making a choice.
Using goods and services to satisfy wants; the ultimate goal of all economic activity.
The scarce inputs used to produce goods and services, also called factors of production: land and raw materials, labor, capital goods and entrepreneurship.
Buildings, tools, machines and equipment that a business uses to produce other goods and services.
The people who work to produce goods and services, along with their physical and mental effort, skills and knowledge.
Raw materials found in nature, such as land, water, minerals and timber, that are used in production.
A business's duty to act in the best interests of society, including its customers, employees and community.
The amount for which buyers and sellers actually exchange a product at a given time, set by supply and demand.
The cost of one product compared with the cost of another, expressed as a ratio.
Handling a possible loss by refusing to take part in the activity that could cause it.
Handling a possible loss by taking steps that lower the chance it will occur, such as screening job applicants or training workers.
Handling a possible loss by shifting it to another party, such as through insurance, bonding, warranties or contracts.
Handling a possible loss by accepting it and paying for any loss out of the business's own funds.
An economic system in which individuals own resources and businesses and make their own economic choices, driven by profit and competition.
The amount of output produced from a given amount of input, calculated as outputs divided by inputs.
The money left after a business pays all its expenses; the owner's reward for taking business risk.
A market condition in which demand exceeds supply, so sellers can charge higher prices.
A market condition in which supply exceeds demand, so prices fall and buyers have more bargaining power.
The desire to earn money that encourages people to start, invest in and grow businesses.
A situation in which the quantity customers buy changes greatly when price changes, typical of luxuries and products with many substitutes.
Rivalry between businesses that sell the same or very similar products to the same customers.
Rivalry between businesses that sell different products that satisfy the same customer need or want.
Intangible activities performed for customers, such as repairs, haircuts or admission to an event, that are produced and consumed at the same time.
The usefulness a product has for satisfying wants, added by business activities that change its form, place, timing, ownership or information.
A possible loss that insurers will not cover because its likelihood or cost cannot be predicted, such as changing customer buying habits.
The four major functions every business performs: production, marketing, management and finance.
Products bought by businesses for use in their operations or in making other products, rather than by final consumers.
An economic system in which the government owns most resources and decides what, how and for whom to produce.
The ability to recognize, understand and manage your own emotions and to recognize and respond effectively to the emotions of others.
Recognizing your own emotions as they occur, including physical signals, and understanding how they affect your behavior and other people.
Information from others about your performance or behavior that shows you what to keep doing and what to improve.
Specific, tactfully delivered feedback that focuses on job performance or behavior and points out ways to improve.
Reacting to criticism by justifying, denying or making excuses, which keeps a person from hearing and using the feedback.
Seeing what needs to be done and doing it, or seeking out additional duties, without being told.
Being accountable for your duties: knowing and performing your job tasks well, following rules and accepting the results of your actions.
Accepting ownership of your own decisions, actions and mistakes, and their results, instead of making excuses or blaming others.
The ability to manage your feelings, words and actions, especially under stress, so you respond thoughtfully rather than react.
A hopeful, constructive outlook that focuses on the good side of people and situations and on solutions rather than complaints.
The ability to adjust your thinking, behavior and plans effectively when tasks, technology, people or priorities change.
Comfort with uncertainty: staying calm, productive and decisive when information is incomplete or outcomes cannot be known.
Expressing your needs, opinions and feelings directly and honestly while respecting the rights and opinions of others.
An oversimplified belief that all members of a group, such as an age group, gender or culture, share the same traits.
A preference for or against a person, group or idea that can prevent fair, objective judgment.
Confidence that another person will be honest, reliable and act in your best interest; it builds slowly and is lost quickly.
Consistently acting on your moral principles and stated values, even when no one is watching or doing so is inconvenient.
The moral principles people use to decide what is right and wrong; in business, they guide decisions and behavior at work.
A situation in which a person must choose between options that conflict with values, duties or interests, with no clearly right choice.
A broad, long-term mental picture of what you want to become and achieve, which guides your goals and choices.
Opinions that differ from your own; considering them means hearing them in full and evaluating them fairly before making a decision.
Opposition by people to new methods, conditions or ideas, most often caused by fear of the unknown.
The overall value or worth you place on yourself, which shapes how you think, act and respond to challenges and other people.
Belief in your own talents, skills and judgment, shown in how you speak, carry yourself, make decisions and handle mistakes.
Treating people impartially by applying the same rules and standards consistently to everyone and basing decisions on facts rather than favoritism.
Controlling impulses and directing emotions productively so you stay motivated, positive and adaptable under pressure.
Recognizing other people's emotions, needs and concerns in a situation; empathy is its central skill.
Using awareness of your own and others' emotions to communicate clearly, resolve conflict, build trust and lead.
Negative feedback that attacks the person, often with insults or labels, instead of focusing on performance and how to improve.
Failing to stand up for your own rights by keeping your needs and opinions to yourself and letting others decide.
Pursuing your own needs or goals in ways that ignore or attack the rights and feelings of others.
A strong drive to meet or exceed standards of excellence, marked by persistence and by setting challenging but reachable goals.
Putting off tasks, especially unpleasant ones, until the last minute or later instead of doing them when they should be done.
A habit of blaming other people or circumstances for your problems, which gives up personal control over your results.
Openly sharing information, including drawbacks and the reasons behind decisions, so others can judge for themselves.
Protecting private information entrusted to you and sharing it only with people who are authorized and need to know.
Awareness of and respect for differences in values, customs, communication styles and beliefs among people of different backgrounds.
The differences among people in a group or workplace, such as age, ethnicity, gender, education and work experience.
Preferring the current or usual way of doing things even when a better option is available.
Going along with a group's decision against your own judgment to keep harmony, which often leads to poor decisions.
A common picture, held by a group, of what a business or team can become, which unites members' efforts.
Anything that keeps a message from being understood as intended, such as incorrect word choice, poor timing or noise.
Disagreement over how to perform work, such as the approach to a task, which can lead to better results when handled well.
A conflict outcome in which each side gives up something to reach an agreement both can accept.
The ability to influence and guide others toward shared goals; it can come from any position, not only a job title.
Beliefs about what is important and right that guide a person's choices, priorities and behavior.
Honestly evaluating your own strengths, weaknesses, interests and values in order to improve performance and set goals.
Saying or doing the right thing to avoid offending others, especially when delivering unwelcome information.
The informal ways people use relationships, influence and power within an organization to advance personal or group interests.
A person whose behavior others look to and imitate; leaders are imitated whether or not they intend to be.
A lack of interest or concern toward work or customers, such as salespeople ignoring shoppers; a negative attitude to avoid.
A conflict response in which a person avoids the other party or the issue, leaving the disagreement unresolved.
A conflict response in which a person gives in to the other side to keep the peace, setting aside his or her own needs.
A conflict response in which one person pushes his or her own solution through at the other person's expense.
A resolution that meets the needs of both parties, usually reached by collaborating to solve the problem together.
Differences people are born with or cannot easily change, such as age, race, ethnicity, gender and physical abilities.
Differences people acquire or can change, such as education, work experience, income, religion and geographic location.
The physical, mental and emotional characteristics that make up a person's personality; many can be developed with effort.
Data about a business's income, expenses, assets and debts that owners, managers and outside groups use to make decisions and judge performance.
An arrangement to receive money, goods or services now in exchange for a promise to pay for them later, usually with interest.
A credit account with a set limit that can be used repeatedly, requiring at least a minimum monthly payment and charging interest on unpaid balances.
Credit for a set amount, often for a costly item, repaid in equal, regular payments over a fixed period of time.
Raising money for a business by selling ownership shares, such as stock, rather than borrowing.
A goal that is specific, measurable, attainable, relevant and time-bound.
Unplanned purchases of wants driven by emotion rather than need, a common obstacle to reaching savings goals.
The principle that a dollar today is worth more than a dollar in the future because money available now can earn interest.
A general rise in prices over time that reduces the purchasing power of money.
Total earnings for a pay period before any taxes or other deductions are subtracted.
Take-home pay that remains after all taxes and other deductions are subtracted from gross pay.
The function of money that allows it to be traded for goods and services, replacing barter.
The function of money that lets it be saved and used to make purchases in the future.
The function of money that expresses the worth of goods and services as prices so their values can be compared.
Currency that has value because a government declares it legal tender, not because it is backed by gold or another commodity.
The process of comparing your own account records with the bank statement to confirm both show the same balance and to catch errors.
A record of a person's borrowing and repayment history that lenders, landlords and employers may review.
The use of another person's personal information, such as a Social Security number or account number, without permission to commit fraud.
The amount a policyholder pays regularly to an insurance company to keep a policy in force.
A tax placed on specific goods, such as gasoline, tobacco or alcohol, often charged as a set amount per unit.
The amount a policyholder must pay out of pocket on a loss before insurance coverage begins to pay.
A fixed amount an insured person pays each time they receive a covered service, such as a doctor's visit.
Raising money for a business by borrowing funds that must be repaid with interest.
The process of choosing which long-term projects or major purchases to fund based on their estimated value to the business.
Interest earned on both the original principal and the interest already added to it.
The price paid for using someone else's money, usually stated as a percentage of the amount borrowed or saved.
The yearly cost of credit, including interest and certain fees, stated as a percentage so loans can be compared.
Money received in exchange for work performed, such as wages, salary, commission, tips and vacation pay.
Money received from sources other than work, such as interest on savings, dividends, rent or gifts.
A running total of pay or deductions from the start of the calendar year through the current pay period.
A percentage of the purchase price of goods and services that retailers collect from customers and send to the government.
A check that has been written and recorded in the register but has not yet cleared the bank.
A company that collects consumers' borrowing and repayment information and sells credit reports to lenders and others.
The system of recording, classifying, summarizing, analyzing and reporting a business's financial transactions.
Things of value that a business or person owns, such as cash, accounts receivable, inventory and equipment.
Debts or financial obligations owed to others, such as accounts payable and loans.
A not-for-profit financial cooperative owned by its members that offers savings, checking and loan services.
A share of ownership in a corporation; shareholders may earn dividends and gains but face the most price volatility.
A loan an investor makes to a company or government in exchange for interest payments and repayment at maturity.
A pension plan that guarantees retirees a set payout, usually based on salary and years of service.
A payment card that withdraws money directly from the holder's checking account at the time of purchase.
The owner's claim on business assets after all liabilities are paid; assets minus liabilities.
A financial statement showing a business's assets, liabilities and owner's equity on a specific date.
A for-profit financial institution that accepts deposits and offers checking, savings, loans and business services.
A securities broker who provides investment advice and research along with trades, charging higher commissions than discount brokers.
Property a borrower pledges to secure a loan, which the lender may take if the loan is not repaid.
A cost that stays the same from one budget period to the next, such as rent or a car payment.
A cost that changes from one budget period to the next, such as groceries, gasoline or entertainment.
The payee's signature on the back of a check, required to cash or deposit it.
The number of days it takes a business to turn money spent on inventory back into cash from sales; shorter is better.
The process of gathering, organizing, storing, protecting and retrieving information so it is accurate and available when people need it.
Software that stores large amounts of related information in an organized way so records can be quickly searched, sorted and retrieved.
A request that tells a database to find and display only the records that meet criteria the user sets.
An online tool that scans indexed web pages and returns a list of those matching the words a user enters.
Software that locates, retrieves and displays web pages on a computer or mobile device.
The specific words or phrases a user types into a search engine to describe the information being sought.
Connecting words such as AND, OR and NOT that tell a search engine how to combine terms to narrow or broaden results.
Software that organizes numeric data in rows and columns of cells and uses formulas to perform calculations automatically.
A set of interrelated programs that share data so a business can handle functions such as inventory, invoicing and accounting together.
The degree to which an information source can be trusted, judged by the author's expertise and the material's accuracy, currency and objectivity.
The unique, registered address that people type into a browser to reach a website, such as example.com.
A company that stores a website's files on its servers and makes the site available on the internet.
The main or opening page of a website, which every other page on the site should link back to.
The physical parts of a computer system, such as the processor, monitor, keyboard and storage drives.
The programs and instructions that tell a computer's physical equipment what tasks to perform.
A condition in which a person or business has more information than it can effectively process, making decisions harder.
The analysis of large amounts of stored data to discover patterns and relationships that turn raw data into useful business information.
Temporary computer memory that holds the programs and files currently in use; its contents are lost when power is turned off.
A storage device that permanently keeps a computer's programs and data, even when the computer is turned off.
The main program that manages a computer's hardware and software resources and lets users run applications.
Productivity software, such as digital calendars, contact lists and reminders, that helps users organize schedules and manage time.
Software for building slide shows that combine text, graphics, sound and animation, often using templates for a uniform design.
Software for creating, editing and formatting text documents such as letters, memos, reports and contracts.
The practice of changing values in a spreadsheet to project how a change, such as a sales increase, would affect other figures.
Clickable text or an image on a web page that takes the user to another page, file or website.
HTML codes placed in a web page's header that describe the page's content, often to help search engines.
The condition of a storage medium or file format becoming outdated, so stored information can no longer be opened or read.
A statement that can be checked and proved true with objective evidence.
A statement of personal belief, feeling or preference that cannot be proved true or false.
Restating only the main points of a piece of information in your own, shorter words.
An information system that records and processes a business's routine daily transactions, such as sales, orders and payments.
Keeping files on internet-based servers so authorized users can reach them anytime, anywhere with an internet connection.
Converting data into a code that only authorized users with the correct key can read, protecting information from theft.
The ongoing, day-to-day activities a business performs to keep running and to turn inputs into the goods and services it sells.
Planning, organizing, and controlling the processes and resources a business uses to create its goods and services efficiently.
The process of creating, growing, manufacturing, or improving goods and services so that they have value for customers.
A manufacturing process that runs nonstop to turn out large volumes of identical goods for steady demand, such as gasoline.
A manufacturing process that stops and starts, making goods in short runs for seasonal, custom, or changing demand.
The business activity of buying the goods and services a company needs to operate or resell, at the right quality, quantity, price, and time.
A buying structure in which a central office, such as company headquarters, makes the buying decisions for all of a company's locations.
A buying structure in which buying authority is delegated to individual stores, districts, or departments; useful when locations are far apart.
An inventory system that updates stock counts continuously, every time an item is received, used, or sold.
The federal agency that sets and enforces workplace safety and health standards and requires employers to provide workplaces free of recognized hazards.
Any condition or action, such as a spill, clutter, or untrained use of equipment, that could cause injury, illness, or damage.
Creations of the mind, such as inventions, brand names, designs, and written works, that the law protects from unauthorized use.
Any person or group affected by or interested in a project or business, such as customers, employees, owners, or community members.
The resources, such as employees, materials, money, equipment, and information, that a business uses to produce goods and services.
Planning and managing the movement and storage of goods, from receiving materials to delivering finished products to customers.
The money, buildings, machinery, tools, and equipment a business uses to produce goods and services.
Deciding in advance what, how, and how much to make, often based on a sales forecast, and scheduling the resources needed.
Buying goods and services that a business will use in its own operations or production rather than resell to customers.
A buyer's written document that authorizes a purchase and states the items, quantities, prices, and delivery terms agreed with a vendor.
Insurance, required in most states, that pays medical costs and lost wages for employees injured or made ill by their jobs.
Theft of merchandise from a store by a person posing as a customer during business hours.
Taking money or property directly from a person by using force, violence, or threats.
A security control that divides cash-handling and recordkeeping tasks among different employees so no single person can steal and hide the theft.
A government grant giving an inventor the exclusive right to make, use, and sell an invention for a set period, usually 20 years.
A step taken to bring an off-track project or process back in line with its plan, such as refocusing scope or adjusting the schedule.
Unlawfully entering a building, often after business hours, with the intent to steal.
Confidential business information, such as a recipe, formula, or process, that gives a company an advantage because competitors do not know it.
The accuracy, completeness, and consistency of data, maintained by protecting it from unauthorized or accidental changes.
An actual count of the items on hand, done by hand or with scanners, to check the accuracy of inventory records.
The specific work, deliverables, and boundaries a project includes; refocusing it is a common corrective action.
Judging a finished effort's results against its objectives, such as comparing projected to actual sales and spending, to guide future work.
Tasks that require immediate attention because they are urgent and important, so they come first when you prioritize work.
Business expenses, such as rent and insurance, that stay the same regardless of how much a company produces or sells.
Knowledge of your own interests, values, personality traits, strengths and weaknesses, which helps you make realistic choices such as selecting a suitable career.
A natural ability or potential to learn a particular skill quickly and well, which assessment surveys can measure objectively.
Following a professional through a typical workday to observe the tasks, skills and work environment of that occupation firsthand.
The career cluster that includes general management, human resources management, operations management, administrative services and business information management careers.
The marketing career area responsible for promotional messages, including advertising, public relations and special events, that inform and persuade audiences.
A person who creates, organizes and runs a new business and assumes its financial risk in hopes of earning a profit.
Not having enough money to start, operate or grow a business; a leading cause of new business failure.
Creating new goods or services, or redesigning existing ones, such as developing new software or an improved appliance.
Changing how a product is made or delivered, such as adding automation or a faster ordering system, to improve efficiency or quality.
Changing the context in which an existing product is presented or the market it targets, without changing the product itself.
A change in the underlying way people or society think about a product, business or industry, such as viewing cars as on-demand services.
A concise written summary of your contact information, education, work experience, skills and achievements, used to win a job interview.
People, such as former employers or teachers, who agree to tell an employer about your character, skills and work habits.
A letter, also called a cover letter, that accompanies a resume, names the position you want and explains how your qualifications fit the employer's needs.
An employer's standard form requesting personal information, education, work history, availability and references, used to screen and compare applicants fairly.
A temporary position, paid or unpaid, that gives students supervised, practical experience in a career field.
Unpaid service to an organization or community that builds skills, references and work experience for your resume.
A formal meeting in which an employer evaluates an applicant's qualifications and communication skills while the applicant learns about the job and company.
The daily habits of keeping your body clean and well groomed, such as bathing, oral care and neat hair, that affect how others see you.
A company's written rules for acceptable employee clothing, grooming and accessories at work.
Working in an orderly, planned way, such as organizing tasks and following procedures, so work is accurate, efficient and consistent.
Courses and training taken after formal schooling ends to keep job knowledge and skills current as technology and jobs change.
An employee benefit in which the employer repays some or all of the cost of approved courses an employee completes.
A specific result you plan to achieve in the near future, usually within a year or less and sometimes as soon as this week.
A result that takes several years of planned effort to achieve, often reached through a series of smaller, nearer goals.
A written plan for reaching a goal that begins by stating the goal and then lists the steps, resources and deadlines needed.
A choice made quickly and almost automatically out of habit, such as what to eat for breakfast.
A choice made only occasionally that requires some thought and information, such as selecting a shop to repair a bike.
A major, often costly or long-lasting choice that requires careful research and comparison of alternatives, such as hiring a manager.
The line of authority in an organization that shows who reports to whom, directing employees to take concerns to their immediate supervisor first.
A document that explains a company's policies, procedures, benefits and expectations for its employees.
Standards describing how employees must behave at work, covering honesty, attendance, safety, respect for others and use of company property.
Unwelcome sexual advances, remarks or conduct at work that create a hostile environment or affect employment decisions; it is illegal.
Building and maintaining professional relationships with people who can share information, advice and referrals that lead to job opportunities.
